title: Small sangats
hookLine: where two or three gather to remember
tomorrow: Navi stops showing up on Tuesdays. what does good company do now?

cards: When a big group chat splits into three small ones, it usually means a fight. In one old Sikh story, the splitting is the blessing. Guru Nanak and Bhai Mardana, his companion with the rabab, walk into a village at dusk.
Nobody offers water. People mock the strangers and shut their doors. As they leave, Guru Nanak blesses the village: may you stay settled right here.
The next village runs out to meet them, feeds them, asks for a song. As they leave, Guru Nanak says: may you be scattered. Mardana stops on the road.
Bless the rude ones to stay, and scatter the kind?

teach.b: Guru Nanak's answer, as the sakhi tells it: if the rude stay where they are, their ways stay put too. If the kind scatter, they carry what they have everywhere they land.
Each family becomes a small sangat in a new place, a lamp set down in another room.

The story comes from the janamsakhis, the life stories of Guru Nanak that Sikhs have told and retold, and versions differ in the details. What holds steady is the picture: the good spreads by being small and moving.
Guru Nanak's own sangat on the road was two people, a singer and a rabab player. Small and true beats big and empty, and a few people who remember together can carry more than a crowd that doesn't.
Simran feels this on Tuesday night.
After the food bank shift, she, Maya and Navi, a quiet kid who stacks cans beside her, sit in the parking lot with a gutka open on the dashboard. Three people, one bani, ten minutes.
Nobody would call it a gathering. Guru Nanak would call it scattered seed.

how: Sikhs gather in small groups at home, on campuses and at work to read a bani, sing a shabad or do a sehaj path together, alongside the larger sangat at the gurdwara.

o: two or three people gathered to remember together
a children's class held before the main service
a gurdwara too small to hold a full langar

games.q: the two villages — tap the pairs.
p: Guru Nanak's companion with the rabab

s: in the story, Guru Nanak curses the rude village
he blesses it to stay settled, so its ways stay put; the kind are scattered to carry the good.
versions of the janamsakhi stories differ in their details
they were told and retold; the picture holds steady while details vary.
a sangat has to be large to matter
the Guru's own road sangat was two people; small and true carries far.

games.q: you're Mardana on the road. the Guru has just blessed the kind village to scatter. what do you think he means?
o: scattered, the kind carry the good to every place they land.
it's a test: the kind will be rewarded later for losing their homes.
it's a rebuke: the kind village was too proud of its kindness.
games.why: as the sakhi tells it, the rude stay put so their ways don't spread; the kind scatter, and each family becomes a small sangat somewhere new.

practice: Sit as you would in a sangat: cross-legged on the floor if your body likes it, or upright on a chair, hands resting in your lap, head covered if that's your way.
Hold the posture the whole sit, as if two others sat in a small circle with you, close enough to hear one another breathe.

wordCard.voice: Small sangats. Two or three people gathered to remember, carrying the good wherever they land.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: rabab, the stringed instrument tradition says Bhai Mardana played for Guru Nanak's hymns.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: small and true, three people and a gutka, scattered like the kind village. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Janamsakhi tradition: Guru Nanak blesses the inhospitable village to stay settled and the hospitable village to be scattered
